extracted.intended_audience: teachers and directors of infant and elementary schools
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions for school teachers/directors to detect, respond to, exclude, and readmit children with infectious or contagious diseases; includes early signs to watch for, disease-specific recognition, isolation and readmission rules, and vaccination advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate personal attention to ill children
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher or director of the school is urged to give immediate personal attention to any child in the school who may appear ill, or who complains of feeling unwell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On noticing illness the teacher should specially note the presence of one or more of the following signs: (1) increased temperature detected by hand on chest/armpit/face/forehead; (2) quickening of pulse with hardness of beat; (3) shivering or increased sweating not due to exercise; (4) great thirst with loss of appetite; (5) tongue white/dry/red; (6) flushed or pallid face; (7) increased or diminished brilliancy of the eye; (8) general weariness, aching loins, headache, drowsiness/excitement, or delirium. "The majority of the above-named symptoms will almost invariably indicate the presence of a febrile state."

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of health required after prolonged absence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any child kept at home away from school for a week or more by its parents should, before returning to its school, bring a certificate of health signed by a duly qualified medical practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-pox detection, vaccination, and readmission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Small-pox sets in with fever, vomiting, and pains in the loins; after not less than two days (commonly on the third) an eruption appears beginning on the face and later forming pustules with a depressed center which terminate in scabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vaccination: "Whenever possible, the teacher should have all the children over ten years revaccinated, especially in times of epidemic small-pox." (Refutes the assertion that revaccination develops small-pox.) Readmission: scabs should have completely disappeared before the child is allowed to return to school; before readmission the child should have had two or three baths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chicken-pox recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicken-pox is a mild disease occasionally preceded by fever, characterized by successive crops of pea-sized blebs/blisters preceded by red spots; blisters contain watery liquid that becomes thick/muddy/bloody and terminates with scabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New crops often appear toward evening; when spots on body are not numerous or well marked, eruption is usually observed among the hair of the head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measles recognition and short exclusion guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Measles begins with general indisposition, fever, sneezing, weeping, red eyes, loud noisy cough, sometimes epistaxis and diarrhoea; after three or four days an eruption appears as small irregular rose-red slightly elevated spots beginning on chin and face and spreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complaint is highly contagious. "While, after ten days' isolation and the use of a bath at the close, a child convalescent from measles may be allowed to associate with others."

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarlet fever recognition and long exclusion requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Scarlet fever commences with extreme general indisposition, high fever, dry burning skin, throat pains and vomiting, followed toward the end of the first day's illness by a raspberry-red rash often covering the body or in patches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eruption shows innumerable round points and may run into minute bladders; the disease varies from mild to virulent; skin peeling may follow. Isolation/readmission: "Not less than six weeks' isolation is required to exhaust the communicability of a case of scarlet fever."

rubrics_metrics.name: Mumps recognition and potential complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mumps may be sudden or preceded by a few days' indisposition and sometimes high fever; stiffness about the jaws followed by bulky tense swelling, usually one side then the other; swelling contains no fluid and dental pain is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swelling may extend behind or under the jaw and sometimes similar swellings occur elsewhere (genital organs liable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ulcerative stomatitis identification and contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ulcerative stomatitis is contagious; its invasion may be preceded by general indisposition usually without fever; grayish bleeding ulcers attack edges of gums, inner cheeks and lips, roof of palates, with extremely fetid breath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diphtheritic sore-throat (croup) detection and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diphtheritic sore-throat or croup is eminently contagious, often commencing insidiously with difficulty in swallowing and slight hoarseness; glands at the angle of the jaw may swell, and a skin- or leather-like false membrane (grayish/whitish/blackened) may appear on the tonsils and soft palate and spread, possibly reaching the windpipe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine with a spoon to press down the tongue and look for the false membrane. This condition must not be confounded with false/spasmodic croup.

rubrics_metrics.name: False (spasmodic) croup distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: False croup typically occurs suddenly at night in a child who was well during the day, with alarming signs of threatened suffocation, loud clamorous coughing and a clear voice; no false membrane and jaw glands not swollen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False croup is generally mild and is not contagious; do not confuse it with diphtheritic croup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dysentery detection and infection-control in school facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dysentery may be contagious; characterized by frequent/continual desire to defecate with only a little slime or mucus often streaked with blood, accompanied by general indisposition and colicky belly pains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To stop infection, no child suffering with dysentery should be allowed to use the general school water or other closet. Dysentery is distinct from diarrhoea (more frequent liquid motions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoid fever early signs and exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Typhoid fever is infectious and may set in with ill-defined signs: loss of appetite and energy, fatigue; then fever with head noises, confusion, obtuse hearing, giddiness, difficulty keeping upright position, epistaxis, colicky belly pains and swelling with diarrhoea, dry hot skin, fouled tongue with red tip and sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The child will generally have already ceased attending school due to indisposition before severe signs appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whooping-cough recognition and mandatory isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whooping-cough is eminently contagious; often preceded by occasional violent fits of coughing over one or more weeks, most frequent at night; fits involve violent successive throbs threatening suffocation followed by a whistling convulsive inspiration and possible vomiting or expectoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owing to grave and fatal complications especially in young children, immediate isolation of the sufferer from its schoolfellows is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ophthalmia (catarrhal and purulent) recognition and contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Both catarrhal and purulent ophthalmia are highly contagious at all ages (especially in very young children); purulent ophthalmia may cause loss of one or both eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eyes and lids become red, swollen, and bathed with a more or less offensive discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scabies (itch) identification and contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Itch is characterized by minute transparent vesicles producing lively itching especially at night; spaces between toes/fingers and wrists most liable; frequent scratching converts rash into scabs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cause: insect (Acarus scabei or Sarcoptes), nocturnal in habit. Though highly contagious, itch can be cured in a few hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crusted ringworm (Tinea favosa) exclusion until medical certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: Crusted ringworm (favosa) is caused by a vegetable parasite frequenting the scalp; hair becomes thin and fragile with irregular puckered yellowish crust-like scabs which crumble to dust and spread contagion; affected heads have peculiar fetid odor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until quite cured, every child suffering from favus should be separated from schoolfellows, and only be readmitted on presenting a proper medical certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ringworm (Tinea tonsurans) identification and contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ringworm is very contagious; hair becomes thinner, fragile, less colored and appears clipped off above skin level; patches are rough, irregular, shaggy, covered with grayish scurfy powder and vary in size from small coins to larger areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several patches may fuse to affect a greater portion of the scalp; itching increases spread through scratching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ringworm with baldness (Tinea decalvans) recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ringworm with baldness presents defined patches naked of hair with glistening ivory whiteness resembling a scar; sizes vary from small coin upward and itching often precedes hair loss; other hairy parts may be affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In children and adults with thick hair this disease may remain long undetected.
